metadata.name: eks
metadata.overview:
Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service is a managed Kubernetes service for running containerized applications in the AWS cloud and in on-premises environments. AWS operates a dedicated, highly available Kubernetes control plane for each cluster and handles its scaling, patching, and recovery. Because the service is conformant with upstream Kubernetes, existing applications and community tooling can typically run without refactoring.

Workloads can run on AWS-managed or self-managed compute in AWS Regions, and on infrastructure in your own data centers or edge locations. An optional automated mode extends AWS management to worker nodes, including provisioning, scaling, operating system patching, networking, load balancing, and block storage.

The service connects Kubernetes access control with AWS Identity and Access Management to help govern cluster access and the AWS permissions workloads receive. AWS-managed tooling also supports GitOps continuous delivery, Kubernetes-native management of AWS resources, and composition of reusable infrastructure building blocks. Integrations with logging, monitoring, encryption, and threat detection services help you observe and protect your clusters.
useCases: Run highly available web applications and microservices across multiple Availability Zones, using managed load balancing and service discovery to route traffic between services.
Train, fine-tune, and serve machine learning models on GPU and accelerator-backed nodes that scale automatically with demand.

Build an internal developer platform where teams deploy applications from Git and provision AWS resources such as databases and storage buckets through Kubernetes-native workflows with organizational guardrails.
Operate a consistent Kubernetes platform across the AWS cloud, on-premises data centers, edge sites, and air-gapped environments using the same cluster tooling and access model.
Run cost-efficient batch processing and big data jobs, such as Apache Spark pipelines, on interruptible Spot capacity.

relationshipToOtherNamespaces.relationship: Worker nodes (managed node groups, self-managed nodes, Auto Mode EC2 managed instances) run as EC2 instances. Clusters require customer VPC subnets and security groups, and EKS places cross-account ENIs in those subnets. Launch templates, IMDS settings, PrivateLink interface endpoints, Transit Gateway and Local/Wavelength Zones are all EC2/VPC constructs.

Nodes and Fargate pull container images, including those for built-in networking add-ons, from Amazon ECR. The node role needs AmazonEC2ContainerRegistryPullOnly, and private clusters need ECR API/DKR endpoints.
Nodes may pull images from ECR Public (public.ecr.aws); AmazonElasticContainerRegistryPublicReadOnly is recommended to avoid rate limiting.

Destination for control plane logs (api, audit, authenticator, controllerManager, scheduler) in /aws/eks/<cluster>/cluster. Auto Mode managed component logs and EKS Capabilities controller logs are delivered as CloudWatch Vended Logs.
Monitoring of clusters and workloads through Container Insights and metrics; alarms are recommended for customer managed KMS key state.

Envelope encryption of all Kubernetes API data with an AWS owned key or a customer managed key (KMS v2 provider; requires kms:CreateGrant/DescribeKey). Customer managed keys can also encrypt Auto Mode root volumes. Disabling or deleting the key degrades the cluster.

Provides the cluster, node, Fargate Pod execution, capability and Pod Identity roles, plus EKS service-linked roles. IAM principals authenticate to the Kubernetes API through access entries or aws-auth, and IRSA relies on an IAM OIDC identity provider.
kubectl authentication tokens are pre-signed STS GetCallerIdentity URLs. IRSA exchanges projected tokens through AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity, and private clusters need an STS VPC endpoint.
Sibling Amazon EKS Auth API. The EKS Pod Identity Agent calls AssumeRoleForPodIdentity to obtain temporary pod credentials, and a dedicated eks-auth interface endpoint exists.
Records all EKS API calls, including capability operations and KMS health-check calls made by the API server.
A Network Load Balancer fronts the control plane. Auto Mode and the AWS Load Balancer Controller provision ALBs and NLBs for Kubernetes Services and Ingress.
GuardDuty EKS Protection analyzes Kubernetes audit logs. Runtime Monitoring uses a GuardDuty agent installed as an EKS add-on (not available on hybrid nodes).
Investigates EKS cluster and Kubernetes API activity using the optional EKS audit logs data source.
Centralizes EKS audit logs, normalized to OCSF, for security analytics; requires control plane logging.
Backs up EKS cluster state and attached EBS, EFS and S3 persistent storage; requires API or API_AND_CONFIG_MAP auth mode so it can create access entries.
Infrastructure-as-code provisioning of the 10 AWS::EKS resource types (Cluster, Nodegroup, AccessEntry, PodIdentityAssociation, Capability, etc.).
The Argo CD capability authenticates to GitHub, GitLab and Bitbucket repositories through CodeConnections instead of long-lived tokens.
The Argo CD capability retrieves Git repository credentials from Secrets Manager; workloads can also consume Secrets Manager secrets.
Cross-cluster and cross-VPC service connectivity through the AWS Gateway API Controller.
Assesses EKS cluster and workload resiliency using Kubernetes RBAC access.
Amazon Managed Service for Prometheus collects metrics from clusters and containerized applications.
Runs self-managed nodes on Outposts, or full local clusters with the control plane on Outposts (outpostConfig).
EKS Anywhere subscriptions provision support licenses in AWS License Manager.
The Argo CD capability authenticates users through IAM Identity Center; capability creation sets up Identity Center applications and assignments.
Argo CD RBAC role mappings reference Identity Center users and groups (the CloudFormation create handler calls identitystore:ListUsers/ListGroups).
SSM hybrid activations can supply credentials for hybrid nodes. The EKS Connector agent uses SSM activations and the ssm/ssmmessages endpoints.
IAM Roles Anywhere provides an X.509 PKI-based credential option for hybrid nodes.
Each managed node group is backed by an EC2 Auto Scaling group that EKS manages in the customer account.
Amazon Inspector checks EKS nodes for vulnerabilities and unintended network reachability.
Recommended for security posture assessment of EKS (including Auto Mode) clusters.
The Mountpoint for S3 CSI driver provides application storage. ECR image layers need the S3 gateway endpoint in private clusters. S3 is also a destination for CloudTrail and vended logs.
The EFS CSI driver provides persistent shared file storage for pods.
Block storage for nodes and persistent volumes through the EBS CSI driver and Auto Mode built-in block storage.
CSI drivers for FSx for Lustre, NetApp ONTAP, OpenZFS and File Cache provide application storage.
ARC zonal shift and autoshift move traffic and Auto Mode node provisioning away from impaired Availability Zones (zonalShiftConfig).
AWS Cloud Map supports service discovery for microservices running on EKS.
EKS creates an EKS-managed Route 53 private hosted zone for the private API server endpoint. Private clusters may need a Route 53 endpoint.
AWS Config records six AWS::EKS resource types and provides EKS managed rules and a Security Best Practices for EKS conformance pack.
Optional delivery destination for Auto Mode managed component logs and EKS Capabilities controller vended logs.
Connectivity option for on-premises access to EKS interface endpoints and private clusters, and for hybrid node networks.
Supplies SSL/TLS certificates for load balancers that Auto Mode or the Load Balancer Controller provision.
AWS Batch runs jobs on Amazon EKS clusters.
Amazon EMR on EKS runs Spark and other EMR workloads on EKS clusters.
Optional tracing destination for workloads; private clusters need an X-Ray interface endpoint.
Container network observability: the Network Flow Monitor agent in the cluster collects pod and node network performance metrics.

entities.name: AccessEntry
entities.overview:
An Amazon EKS access entry grants an AWS IAM user or role access to the Kubernetes API of a specific cluster. It links that IAM identity to a Kubernetes username and optional group memberships. IAM authentication then carries through to authorization inside the cluster.

Permissions come from AWS-managed access policies, scoped to the whole cluster or to selected namespaces. Kubernetes role-based access control can also grant permissions through the entry's group memberships. Worker nodes can use entries for their IAM roles to join the cluster with permissions that Amazon EKS supplies.

Access entries let teams manage cluster access with the AWS tools they already use, instead of editing an in-cluster configuration map. Administrators can revoke or narrow access, including the cluster creator's default administrator access, without connecting to the cluster. This helps restore access when in-cluster mappings are misconfigured.

entities.name: Addon
entities.overview:
An Amazon EKS add-on is a managed installation of operational software on an Amazon EKS cluster. It covers supporting components such as networking plugins, cluster DNS, storage drivers, and observability or security agents that applications depend on.

Amazon EKS deploys the software into the cluster, checks version compatibility, and applies updates when you initiate them. You can adjust supported settings, choose a target namespace, and keep your own changes to fields that Amazon EKS does not manage.

Add-ons that call AWS services can receive scoped IAM permissions through a role bound to the add-on's Kubernetes service account. This helps avoid granting the software broad permissions inherited from the cluster's nodes. Add-ons are published by AWS, by AWS Marketplace sellers, and by open source communities, with different levels of validation and support.

entities.name: Capability
entities.overview:
A capability adds a fully managed platform feature to an Amazon EKS cluster. It runs controller software in AWS-managed infrastructure outside the cluster, so worker nodes do not host or scale these components. AWS manages patching, version upgrades, scaling, and availability for the controllers.

Each capability delivers one Kubernetes-native tool as a managed service. Argo CD delivers applications from Git, AWS Controllers for Kubernetes manages AWS resources, and kro composes resources into reusable APIs. Teams work with it through standard Kubernetes custom resources, kubectl, and Git workflows.

A capability acts on your behalf with an IAM role you provide and receives scoped Kubernetes permissions in the cluster. This helps platform teams offer self-service infrastructure and deployments while keeping control over permissions.

entities.name: CertificateAuthority
entities.overview:
An Amazon EKS certificate authority is the root of trust for a cluster's Kubernetes control plane. It signs the certificates that secure API server connections, so worker nodes and clients can verify the API server's identity.

Each cluster receives its own certificate authority at creation, and each certificate authority has a finite validity period. Rotation adds a successor certificate authority, which Amazon EKS distributes to AWS managed components before it can become the signer. During the dual trust period, the cluster trusts both certificate authorities, so you can update nodes and clients incrementally.

Amazon EKS helps keep clusters available by adding and activating a successor automatically as expiration approaches. A limited rollback window lets you revert to the previous signer if a missed client loses connectivity. You remain responsible for updating the worker nodes you manage and your external clients to trust the successor.

entities.name: Cluster
entities.overview:
An Amazon EKS cluster is a managed Kubernetes environment for deploying, scaling, and operating containerized applications. AWS operates a dedicated, highly available control plane for each cluster across multiple Availability Zones. The control plane includes the Kubernetes API server and its backing data store.

The cluster attaches to subnets in your VPC so the control plane can communicate with the nodes that run your workloads. You choose how clients reach the Kubernetes API endpoint, from address-restricted public access to private access within your network. Optionally, EKS can also manage compute capacity, block storage, and load balancing for the cluster.

Cluster settings help you control how AWS identities authenticate to Kubernetes. You can also encrypt Kubernetes data with your own key, export control plane logs, and manage version upgrades. Deletion protection helps guard against accidental removal of the cluster. A cluster can also represent an external Kubernetes cluster connected for visibility in the console.

entities.name: EksAnywhereSubscription
entities.overview:
An EKS Anywhere subscription entitles an AWS account to AWS support for Amazon EKS Anywhere clusters running on customer-managed infrastructure. It also gives the account access to EKS Anywhere Curated Packages, which add capabilities such as load balancing, observability, and autoscaling.

Each subscription includes a fixed number of cluster licenses for a one-year or three-year term. Each license covers a single EKS Anywhere cluster. The licenses are delivered through AWS License Manager, where they can be accepted and applied to clusters. By default, only the purchasing account can access Curated Packages, though access can be shared with other accounts in the same organization.

Subscriptions can renew automatically at the end of each term, and their status shows whether coverage is active, expiring, or expired. After expiration, the licenses no longer cover new support cases, and access to Curated Packages ends.

entities.name: FargateProfile
entities.overview:
A Fargate profile tells an Amazon EKS cluster which Kubernetes pods run on AWS Fargate serverless compute instead of on nodes you manage. Administrators define selectors that match pods by namespace and optional labels, including simple wildcard patterns. When a pod being scheduled matches a selector, EKS runs it on Fargate with that profile's settings.

Each profile also sets the private subnets where matching pods receive their network interfaces. It names a pod execution role that lets the Fargate infrastructure register as a cluster node and pull container images. Each pod runs in its own isolated compute environment, so teams avoid provisioning, patching, or scaling worker nodes.

Profiles cannot be changed after creation. To adjust one, create a replacement profile first and then remove the original. Deleting a profile stops its pods; they reschedule only if another profile matches them.

entities.name: IdentityProviderConfig
entities.overview:
An identity provider config links an Amazon EKS cluster to an external OpenID Connect identity provider. Users can then authenticate to the Kubernetes API with tokens from an existing identity system, alongside or instead of IAM identities.

The configuration names the provider's issuer and the client audience that the cluster trusts. It also maps token claims to Kubernetes user names and groups, and can add prefixes that keep those names distinct. Required claims can be set so that the cluster accepts only tokens carrying expected values.

Authenticated users receive permissions through Kubernetes role-based access control bindings. This helps organizations manage cluster access through their existing identity lifecycle without creating an IAM identity for every developer. Removing the configuration ends access for that provider's users, while IAM-based access to the cluster continues.

entities.name: Nodegroup
entities.overview:
A managed node group provides the Amazon EC2 worker capacity that runs Kubernetes workloads in an Amazon EKS cluster. Amazon EKS provisions the instances through an Auto Scaling group in your account and registers them with the cluster automatically. Each group spans the subnets and Availability Zones you choose.

Amazon EKS handles node lifecycle tasks such as rolling updates to newer Kubernetes or machine image versions. During updates and terminations, nodes are cordoned and drained to help keep applications available. Optional automatic repair can help detect unhealthy nodes and replace or reboot them.

You control the operating system image, instance types, capacity type, scaling limits, Kubernetes labels, and taints. Launch templates allow deeper customization, such as custom images, bootstrap settings, storage encryption, and instance metadata options.

entities.name: PodIdentityAssociation
entities.overview:
A pod identity association links an IAM role to a Kubernetes service account in a specific namespace of an Amazon EKS cluster. Pods that run under that service account receive short-lived AWS credentials for the role, which are rotated automatically. This works much like an instance profile does for an EC2 instance, but at the granularity of individual workloads.

The association helps avoid embedding long-term access keys in containers or relying on the node's role. It can optionally chain to a target role in the same or another account for cross-account access. It can also apply an inline session policy that narrows the role's permissions for that workload.

By default, credentials carry session tags describing the cluster, namespace, service account, and pod. These tags help administrators write attribute-based policies so one role can serve many workloads with different effective access. Associations are managed through Amazon EKS, so no OpenID Connect provider setup or service account annotations are required.

mitigations.statement: Amazon EKS service API calls on a governed VPC network should only be made against trusted resources or AWS service-owned resources

mitigationContext.context: Amazon EKS API calls from your VPCs can target clusters in another account. Restricting those calls to resources in your organization enforces the resource perimeter on your network.

mitigations.statement: Amazon EKS service API calls on a governed VPC network should only be made by trusted identities or AWS services

mitigationContext.context: Amazon EKS API calls from your VPCs can be made by identities outside your organization. Restricting those calls to principals in your organization enforces the identity perimeter on your network.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon EKS cluster's access entry should be tagged with information that describes the owner and purpose

mitigationContext.context: You tag an access entry through the `$.tags{key}` key-to-value map on `CreateAccessEntry` or later through `TagResource`, separately from your cluster's tags. Owner and purpose tags help track ownership and the business function each cluster's access entry supports.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon EKS cluster's addon should be configured to send network policy logs to CloudWatch Logs

mitigationContext.context: The Amazon VPC CNI add-on's network policy agent can record network policy logs of allowed and denied connections, with delivery controlled by the `$.configurationValues` request parameter. Sending those logs to CloudWatch Logs provides security-relevant visibility for audit trails, access monitoring, or error detection.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon EKS cluster's addon's EKS Pod Identity IAM role, or its IAM role for service accounts where no pod identity association applies, should be restricted to accessing resources only from expected networks

mitigationContext.context: Your add-on binds IAM roles to its Kubernetes service accounts through `$.podIdentityAssociations[*].roleArn` (each EKS Pod Identity IAM role) and `$.serviceAccountRoleArn` (the IAM role for service accounts), and its containers call AWS services with the credentials of whichever of those roles applies. Restricting those calls to expected networks enforces the network perimeter on your identities and helps prevent the use of those credentials from unexpected networks.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon EKS cluster's addon's Pod Identity IAM role should be assumed only by Amazon EKS acting on behalf of trusted resources

mitigationContext.context: You can pass a Pod Identity IAM role for your cluster's addon's service account in the `$.podIdentityAssociations[*].roleArn` request parameter, and the role's trust policy specifies which principals can assume it. Allowing only Amazon EKS, acting on behalf of trusted resources, to assume the role helps prevent an unintended principal from assuming it.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon EKS cluster's addon should have Prometheus Node Exporter, kube-state-metrics, EKS node monitoring agent, AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry (ADOT), Container Network Observability performance metrics, SR-IOV Network Metrics Exporter, or Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Observability Add-on enabled to collect detailed non-CloudWatch metrics

mitigationContext.context: Your Amazon EKS cluster's addon can be Prometheus Node Exporter, kube-state-metrics, EKS node monitoring agent, AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry (ADOT), SR-IOV Network Metrics Exporter, Amazon SageMaker HyperPod Observability Add-on, or the AWS Network Flow Monitor Agent with Container Network Observability performance metrics enabled through its configuration values. These features capture detailed operational telemetry, such as hardware and network-device metrics, Kubernetes object state, and node health signals, kept outside Amazon CloudWatch Metrics.

If another monitoring platform already collects equivalent detailed metrics for this resource, that platform can provide the same visibility for anomaly detection and incident response. Enable this feature when no equivalent collection is in place.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon EKS cluster's addon should be tagged with information that describes the owner and purpose

mitigationContext.context: You tag a cluster's addon with the `$.tags{key}` key-to-value map on `CreateAddon` or through `TagResource`, and these tags are separate from the cluster's tags. Owner and purpose tags help track ownership and the business function each cluster's addon supports.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon EKS cluster's addon should have Container Insights with enhanced observability enabled to collect detailed CloudWatch metrics

mitigationContext.context: Setting `$.addonName`, the add-on name, to `amazon-cloudwatch-observability` installs Container Insights with enhanced observability, which publishes cluster, node, pod, container, and control plane metrics beyond the basic `AWS/EKS` metrics. Collecting those metrics improves security visibility by providing finer-grained data for anomaly detection and incident response.

If another monitoring platform already collects equivalent detailed metrics for this resource, that platform can provide the same visibility for anomaly detection and incident response. Enable this feature when no equivalent collection is in place.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon EKS cluster's capability's IAM role should be assumed only by Amazon EKS acting on behalf of trusted resources

mitigationContext.context: The `$.roleArn` request parameter names the capability IAM role that Amazon EKS assumes, and the role's trust policy specifies which principals can assume it. Allowing only Amazon EKS, acting on behalf of trusted resources, to assume the role helps prevent an unintended principal from assuming it.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon EKS cluster's capability that uses AWS IAM Identity Center to authenticate principals should be configured only with trusted IAM Identity Center instances

mitigationContext.context: An Amazon EKS cluster's capability of type Argo CD authenticates users to its hosted Argo CD UI and API through the AWS IAM Identity Center instance set by the `$.configuration.argoCd.awsIdc.idcInstanceArn` request parameter. Configuring only trusted IAM Identity Center instances helps prevent an untrusted identity provider from being used to gain unintended access.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon EKS cluster's capability should be tagged with information that describes the owner and purpose

mitigationContext.context: You tag your cluster's capability through the `$.tags{key}` key-to-value map on `CreateCapability` or by calling `TagResource` on the capability ARN, separately from the cluster. Owner and purpose tags help track ownership and the business function each cluster's capability supports.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon EKS cluster's capability should be configured to send EKS_CAPABILITY_ACK_LOGS, EKS_CAPABILITY_KRO_LOGS, or EKS_CAPABILITY_ARGOCD_* logs to CloudWatch Logs using vended logs delivery

mitigationContext.context: Controller logs record the activity of the ACK, kro, or Argo CD controllers that Amazon EKS runs for your capability outside your cluster. Sending those logs to CloudWatch Logs using vended logs delivery provides security-relevant visibility.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon EKS cluster should be configured to send API server, audit, authenticator, controller manager, and scheduler logs to CloudWatch Logs

mitigationContext.context: Your Amazon EKS cluster's control plane produces API server, audit, authenticator, controller manager, and scheduler logs that record Kubernetes API activity, IAM-based authentication, control loop activity, and Pod scheduling, each exported only when enabled in its logging configuration. Sending those logs to CloudWatch Logs provides security-relevant visibility for audit trails, access monitoring, or error detection.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon EKS cluster's Auto Mode node IAM role and EKS Connector agent IAM role should be restricted to accessing resources only from expected networks

mitigationContext.context: Your EKS Auto Mode cluster's `$.computeConfig.nodeRoleArn` request parameter designates the Auto Mode node IAM role, whose credentials the code on its EC2 managed instances uses to call AWS services, and a registered external cluster's `$.connectorConfig.roleArn` designates the EKS Connector agent IAM role, whose credentials the EKS Connector agent in that connected cluster uses to call AWS services. Restricting those calls to expected networks enforces the network perimeter on your identities and helps prevent the use of those credentials from unexpected networks.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon EKS cluster's service role should be assumed only by Amazon EKS, its Auto Mode node IAM role only by Amazon EC2, and its connector agent IAM role only by AWS Systems Manager, acting on behalf of trusted resources

mitigationContext.context: You pass your cluster's service role in the `$.roleArn` request parameter, you can pass an Auto Mode node IAM role in `$.computeConfig.nodeRoleArn` and a registered cluster's connector agent IAM role in `$.connectorConfig.roleArn`, and each role's trust policy specifies which principals can assume it. Allowing only Amazon EKS, Amazon EC2, and AWS Systems Manager, acting on behalf of trusted resources, to assume those roles helps prevent an unintended principal from assuming them.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon EKS cluster's control plane network interfaces should be placed only in private subnets

mitigationContext.context: The `$.resourcesVpcConfig.subnetIds[*]` request parameter sets your cluster subnets, which hold the cross-account elastic network interfaces connecting your cluster's control plane to your nodes. Private subnet placement helps prevent direct internet routing to your cluster's control plane network interfaces, reducing their network exposure.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon EKS cluster should have the EKS node monitoring agent enabled to collect detailed non-CloudWatch metrics

mitigationContext.context: With EKS Auto Mode compute enabled, your Amazon EKS cluster includes the EKS node monitoring agent in the AMI of every Auto Mode node. This feature captures detailed operational telemetry, such as kernel, container runtime, networking, storage, and accelerated-hardware health issues, kept outside Amazon CloudWatch Metrics.

If another monitoring platform already collects equivalent detailed metrics for this resource, that platform can provide the same visibility for anomaly detection and incident response. Enable this feature when no equivalent collection is in place.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon EKS cluster's control plane instance and etcd instance should use an EC2 instance type that supports automatic encryption of instance-to-instance traffic

mitigationContext.context: A local Amazon EKS cluster runs its Kubernetes control plane and etcd on Amazon EC2 instances that Amazon EKS launches on your Outpost. The instance type you select for the control plane and etcd instances determines whether traffic between those instances can be automatically encrypted in transit, which applies between supported instance types in the same Region on a direct network path.

mitigations.statement: IAM principals should be restricted to accessing only trusted Amazon EKS cluster resources

mitigationContext.context: An access entry on an Amazon EKS cluster in another account can grant your principals access to that cluster's Kubernetes API. Restricting the clusters your principals can access helps keep data access within trusted accounts.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon EKS cluster should be protected by an AWS Backup backup plan

mitigationContext.context: An Amazon EKS cluster stores Kubernetes cluster state and persistent volume data. AWS Backup supports the Amazon EKS cluster as an independently protectable resource type and captures its contents in composite recovery points.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon EKS cluster's Kubernetes API data should be encrypted with an AWS KMS customer managed key

mitigationContext.context: Envelope encryption helps protect the Kubernetes API data, such as Secrets and ConfigMaps, that your Amazon EKS cluster stores in etcd. Through `CreateCluster` or `AssociateEncryptionConfig`, you can use a customer managed key as the key encryption key instead of an AWS owned key. A customer managed key lets you audit its use and control its lifecycle, including deleting it to make the stored data unavailable.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon EKS cluster should use cluster access management API

mitigationContext.context: Amazon EKS supports managing the Kubernetes permissions of IAM principals from outside the cluster through access entries, its cluster access management API. The `aws-auth` ConfigMap, whose accidental deletion or syntax errors can lock users out, is deprecated in favor of access entries.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon EKS cluster should be accessed only by trusted identities or AWS services acting on behalf of trusted resources

mitigationContext.context: Your Amazon EKS cluster supports access entries that specify who can access its Kubernetes API and what actions they can perform. Restricting who can access your clusters helps keep data access within trusted accounts.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon EKS cluster should be tagged with information that describes the owner and purpose

mitigationContext.context: You tag an Amazon EKS cluster through the `$.tags{key}` request parameter, a key-to-value map, when you call `CreateCluster` or later through `TagResource`, and a connected cluster only when you call `RegisterCluster`. Owner and purpose tags help track ownership and the business function each cluster supports.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon EKS cluster should be associated only with security groups whose inbound and outbound rules restrict traffic to only the required sources, destinations, protocols, and ports

mitigationContext.context: Amazon EKS associates the cluster security group it creates with the cross-account elastic network interfaces in your cluster subnets, and you can associate additional groups through `$.resourcesVpcConfig.securityGroupIds[*]`. Restricting the inbound and outbound rules to the required sources, destinations, protocols, and ports helps reduce the network exposure of your cluster.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon EKS cluster should have deletion protection enabled

mitigationContext.context: An Amazon EKS cluster has its own deletion protection setting, `$.deletionProtection`, which you can turn on at creation or later. This setting helps protect the cluster from unintended deletion.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon EKS eks anywhere subscription should be tagged with information that describes the owner and purpose

mitigationContext.context: You tag an eks anywhere subscription through the `$.tags{key}` key-to-value map on `CreateEksAnywhereSubscription`, or later through `TagResource`. Owner and purpose tags help track ownership and the business function each eks anywhere subscription supports.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon EKS cluster's fargate profile's Pod execution role should be restricted to accessing resources only from expected networks

mitigationContext.context: The `$.podExecutionRoleArn` request parameter designates your Fargate profile's Pod execution role, and the Amazon EKS components on the Fargate infrastructure call AWS services with the role's credentials. Restricting those calls to expected networks enforces the network perimeter on your identities and helps prevent the use of those credentials from unexpected networks.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon EKS cluster's Fargate profile's Pod execution role should be assumed only by Amazon EKS acting on behalf of trusted resources

mitigationContext.context: Your cluster's Fargate profile binds a Pod execution role through the required `$.podExecutionRoleArn` request parameter, and the role's trust policy specifies which principals can assume it. Allowing only Amazon EKS, acting on behalf of trusted resources, to assume the role helps prevent an unintended principal from assuming it.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon EKS cluster's fargate profile's Pods should be placed only in private subnets

mitigationContext.context: The `$.subnets[*]` request parameter on `CreateFargateProfile` sets the subnets that hold the Pods your Fargate profile schedules, each with its own elastic network interface. Private subnet placement helps prevent direct internet routing to those Pods, reducing their network exposure.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon EKS cluster's Fargate profile should launch its Pods in subnets in more than one Availability Zone.

mitigationContext.context: Amazon EKS launches each Pod that matches your Fargate profile with its own elastic network interface in a subnet from the `$.subnets[*]` subnet list. Placing those network interfaces in more than one Availability Zone provides network-level redundancy and helps keep connectivity available when one zone is disrupted.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon EKS cluster's fargate profile should be tagged with information that describes the owner and purpose

mitigationContext.context: You can tag your Fargate profile through the `$.tags{key}` key-to-value map on `CreateFargateProfile` or later through `TagResource`, independently of your cluster's tags. Owner and purpose tags help track ownership and the business function each cluster's fargate profile supports.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon EKS cluster's identity provider config that uses OIDC to authenticate principals should be configured only with trusted OIDC identity providers

mitigationContext.context: An Amazon EKS cluster's identity provider config lets users authenticate to the cluster's Kubernetes API through the OpenID Connect (OIDC) identity provider that the `$.oidc.issuerUrl` request parameter designates. Configuring only trusted OIDC identity providers helps prevent an untrusted identity provider from being used to gain unintended access.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon EKS cluster's identity provider config should be tagged with information that describes the owner and purpose

mitigationContext.context: You can tag your cluster's identity provider config through the `$.tags{key}` key-to-value map on `AssociateIdentityProviderConfig` or by calling `TagResource`, separately from your cluster's tags. Owner and purpose tags help track ownership and the business function each cluster's identity provider config supports.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon EKS cluster's nodegroup's node IAM role should be restricted to accessing resources only from expected networks

mitigationContext.context: The `$.nodeRole` request parameter designates your node group's node IAM role, and code on its instances makes AWS API calls with that role's credentials. Restricting those calls to expected networks enforces the network perimeter on your identities and helps prevent the use of those credentials from unexpected networks.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon EKS cluster's nodegroup's node IAM role should be assumed only by Amazon EC2 acting on behalf of trusted resources

mitigationContext.context: Your cluster's nodegroup binds its node IAM role through the `$.nodeRole` request parameter, and the role's trust policy specifies which principals can assume it. Allowing only Amazon EC2, acting on behalf of trusted resources, to assume the role helps prevent an unintended principal from assuming it.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon EKS cluster's nodegroup should be placed only in private subnets

mitigationContext.context: The required `$.subnets[*]` request parameter sets the subnets where your nodegroup's Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling group launches each node and its network interfaces. Private subnet placement helps prevent direct internet routing to your nodegroup's nodes, reducing their network exposure.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon EKS cluster's nodegroup should use an EC2 instance type that supports automatic encryption of instance-to-instance traffic

mitigationContext.context: Your managed node group runs the nodes that host your Pods as Amazon EC2 instances in your AWS account, across the subnets you choose. The instance type you specify for the node group or in its launch template determines whether traffic between your nodes and other instances can be automatically encrypted in transit, which applies between supported instance types in the same Region on a direct network path.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon EKS cluster's nodegroup should launch its nodes in subnets in more than one Availability Zone

mitigationContext.context: The `$.subnets[*]` request parameter lists the subnets where your Amazon EKS managed node group launches its nodes, each with its own network interfaces. Placing those network interfaces in more than one Availability Zone provides network-level redundancy and helps keep connectivity available when one zone is disrupted.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon EKS cluster's nodegroup should be tagged with information that describes the owner and purpose

mitigationContext.context: You can tag your cluster's nodegroup through the `$.tags{key}` key-to-value map on `CreateNodegroup` or `TagResource`, separately from its Auto Scaling group and EC2 instances. Owner and purpose tags help track ownership and the business function each cluster's nodegroup supports.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon EKS cluster's nodegroup should be associated only with security groups whose inbound and outbound rules restrict traffic to only the required sources, destinations, protocols, and ports

mitigationContext.context: Your nodegroup's EC2 instances use the cluster security group by default, or can use custom security groups from the launch template referenced through `$.launchTemplate.id` or `$.launchTemplate.name`. Restricting the inbound and outbound rules to the required sources, destinations, protocols, and ports helps reduce the network exposure of your nodegroup.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon EKS cluster's pod identity association's target IAM role, or its EKS Pod Identity role where no target IAM role is configured, should be restricted to accessing resources only from expected networks

mitigationContext.context: Your pod identity association binds a Kubernetes service account to `$.roleArn` (the EKS Pod Identity role), optionally chained to `$.targetRoleArn` (the target IAM role), and your containers in Pods that use that service account call AWS services with the resulting role credentials. Restricting those calls to expected networks enforces the network perimeter on your identities and helps prevent the use of those credentials from unexpected networks.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon EKS cluster's pod identity association's EKS Pod Identity role should be assumed only by Amazon EKS acting on behalf of trusted resources

mitigationContext.context: The `$.roleArn` request parameter binds your cluster's pod identity association to an EKS Pod Identity role, whose trust policy specifies which principals can assume it. Allowing only Amazon EKS, acting on behalf of trusted resources, to assume the role helps prevent an unintended principal from assuming it.

mitigations.statement: An Amazon EKS cluster's pod identity association should be tagged with information that describes the owner and purpose

mitigationContext.context: You tag your cluster's pod identity association through the `$.tags{key}` key-to-value map on `CreatePodIdentityAssociation` or through `TagResource`, separately from the cluster's own tags. Owner and purpose tags help track ownership and the business function each cluster's pod identity association supports.

threats.prerequisites: operating from a governed VPC network
threats.threatAction: can use the governed VPC network to make Amazon EKS service API calls

threatContext.context: Amazon EKS is reachable from your VPC through an interface VPC endpoint (powered by AWS PrivateLink), for cluster management API calls. An IAM principal from outside your organization can use that network path to make Amazon EKS API calls with its own credentials.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions on untrusted Amazon EKS resources
threats.threatAction: can interact with those untrusted resources from a governed VPC network

threatContext.context: Amazon EKS API calls from your VPCs can target Amazon EKS resources in another account. An IAM principal in that network with permissions on Amazon EKS resources outside your organization can call those operations against them.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to create or modify an Amazon EKS cluster's access entry
threats.threatAction: can configure the access entry without required tagging information

threatContext.context: An IAM principal with permissions to create or modify an Amazon EKS cluster's access entry can omit the required tags, or remove them through `UntagResource`. An Amazon EKS cluster's access entry left without those tags still grants cluster access and may fall outside ownership attribution, cost allocation, and compliance inventory.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to modify an Amazon EKS cluster's addon
threats.threatAction: can disable Container Insights with enhanced observability, node health monitoring, or Prometheus metrics for the addon

threatContext.context: Your Amazon EKS cluster's addon can provide Container Insights with enhanced observability, node health monitoring, or Prometheus metrics beyond the basic `AWS/EKS` metrics. An IAM principal with permission to modify the addon can disable this monitoring, stopping the detailed metrics and node health status it reports.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to create or modify an Amazon EKS cluster's addon
threats.threatAction: can configure the addon without required tagging information

threatContext.context: An IAM principal with permissions to create or modify an Amazon EKS cluster's addon can omit the required tags, or remove them through `UntagResource`. An addon left without those tags still runs on your cluster and may fall outside ownership attribution, cost allocation, and compliance inventory.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to create or modify an Amazon EKS cluster's addon that supports Container Insights with enhanced observability or Container Network Observability performance metrics
threats.threatAction: can create or configure the cluster's addon without Container Insights with enhanced observability or Container Network Observability performance metrics enabled

threatContext.context: An IAM principal can create or update your cluster's addon with `$.configurationValues` that leave Container Insights with enhanced observability or Container Network Observability performance metrics disabled. Without node-, pod-, container- and accelerator-level metrics or network performance metrics, anomalous resource use, such as a cryptomining burst or unexpected traffic, is harder to detect.

threats.prerequisites: that has been granted access to my Amazon EKS cluster's addon's Pod Identity IAM role through its trust policy
threats.threatAction: can assume my Pod Identity IAM role and act with its permissions

threatContext.context: Your Amazon EKS cluster's addon designates an optional Pod Identity IAM role through `$.podIdentityAssociations[*].roleArn`, and you author its trust policy. That trust policy can allow identities outside your organization to assume the role and act with its permissions, including your addon's access to AWS resources.

threats.prerequisites: with possession of credentials for my Amazon EKS cluster's addon's EKS Pod Identity IAM role or IAM role for service accounts
threats.threatAction: can use my EKS Pod Identity IAM role or IAM role for service accounts while on an unexpected network

threatContext.context: When you assign an EKS Pod Identity IAM role or an IAM role for service accounts to your add-on, its pods receive temporary credentials for that role. A threat actor who obtains those credentials can use either role while on an unexpected network.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to use an Amazon EKS cluster
threats.threatAction: can deploy Pods that initiate network connections without a record of those connections being persisted by Amazon VPC CNI network policy logging

threatContext.context: When Amazon VPC CNI network policy logging is not configured on your Amazon EKS cluster's addon, no connection verdict records are written by Amazon VPC CNI network policy logging. An IAM principal with permissions to use the Amazon EKS cluster can deploy Pods that initiate network connections to other Pods and to endpoints outside the cluster, leaving no record of those connections persisted by the VPC CNI network policy logging.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to modify an Amazon EKS cluster's addon
threats.threatAction: can disable network policy logging for the addon

threatContext.context: An IAM principal with permissions to modify your Amazon EKS cluster's addon can call `UpdateAddon` with `$.configurationValues` that turn off `nodeAgent.enablePolicyEventLogs` or `nodeAgent.enableCloudWatchLogs`. Either change stops the `vpc-cni` node agent's opt-in network policy logs from reaching CloudWatch Logs while pod traffic continues under your network policies.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to create or modify an Amazon EKS cluster's capability
threats.threatAction: can configure the capability without required tagging information

threatContext.context: An IAM principal with permissions to create or modify an Amazon EKS cluster's capability can omit the required tags, or remove them through `UntagResource`. An Amazon EKS cluster's capability left without those tags still accrues hourly charges and may fall outside ownership attribution, cost allocation, and compliance inventory.

threats.prerequisites: with knowledge of a flawed AWS IAM Identity Center's external provider configuration
threats.threatAction: can take advantage of the flawed AWS IAM Identity Center's external provider configuration to gain unauthorized access to the Amazon EKS cluster's capability

threatContext.context: For an Argo CD capability's UI and API, the AWS IAM Identity Center instance you choose admits the identities your external identity provider asserts. A defect in that provider configuration's trust relationship, signature validation or identity mappings can let a threat actor gain unauthorized access to the Amazon EKS cluster's capability.

threats.prerequisites: with knowledge of a vulnerable external identity provider configured in an AWS IAM Identity Center instance used by an Amazon EKS cluster's capability
threats.threatAction: can gain federated access to the capability's hosted Argo CD UI and API

threatContext.context: An Amazon EKS cluster's capability delegates authentication for its Argo CD UI and API to the AWS IAM Identity Center instance named in its configuration. If the external identity provider you connect to that IAM Identity Center instance is vulnerable, a threat actor can gain federated access to the capability's hosted Argo CD UI and API.

threats.prerequisites: that has been granted access to my Amazon EKS cluster's capability's IAM role through its trust policy
threats.threatAction: can assume my capability IAM role and act with its permissions

threatContext.context: Your Amazon EKS cluster's capability designates a capability IAM role through `$.roleArn`, and you author its trust policy. That trust policy can allow identities outside your organization to assume the role and act with its permissions.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to use an Amazon EKS cluster's capability
threats.threatAction: can interact with the capability, causing its controllers to act on their behalf, without a record of that controller activity being persisted by vended logs delivery of its EKS_CAPABILITY_ACK_LOGS, EKS_CAPABILITY_KRO_LOGS, or EKS_CAPABILITY_ARGOCD_* controller logs

threatContext.context: When vended logs delivery is not configured on your Amazon EKS cluster's capability, no controller activity logs are written by vended logs delivery. An IAM principal with permissions to use the capability can create resources that its controllers reconcile on their behalf, such as AWS resources through ACK, composed resources through kro, or applications synchronized from a Git repository through Argo CD, leaving no record of those actions persisted by vended logs delivery.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to modify the log delivery configuration for an Amazon EKS capability
threats.threatAction: can disable controller log delivery for the capability

threatContext.context: An IAM principal with permissions to modify the CloudWatch Logs deliveries for your Amazon EKS cluster's capability can call `DeleteDelivery` on each delivery for the capability's ACK, kro or Argo CD controller logs, then `DeleteDeliverySource` on its delivery sources. Deleting those deliveries stops the capability's opt-in controller logs from reaching CloudWatch Logs while its controllers keep reconciling resources; calling `DeleteDelivery` for only some of an Argo CD capability's log types stops those records while its other log types continue.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to delete an Amazon EKS cluster
threats.threatAction: can delete the cluster and the Kubernetes objects that the cluster contains

threatContext.context: An Amazon EKS cluster holds your Kubernetes objects. An IAM principal with permission to delete the cluster can delete that data along with it through the `DeleteCluster` operation, without Kubernetes role-based access control (RBAC) permissions to delete those objects.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to delete an Amazon EKS cluster
threats.threatAction: can delete the cluster

threatContext.context: An IAM principal with permissions to delete an Amazon EKS cluster can call `DeleteCluster` with the cluster's name in `$.name`. That call deletes the cluster and removes its Kubernetes control plane and cluster state, ending orchestration and Kubernetes API access for your workloads.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to modify an Amazon EKS cluster
threats.threatAction: can disable the EKS node monitoring agent on EKS Auto Mode nodes for the cluster

threatContext.context: The EKS node monitoring agent on EKS Auto Mode nodes reports kernel, container runtime, networking, storage, and accelerated hardware health beyond default CloudWatch metrics. An IAM principal with permission to modify the cluster can disable it, by turning off EKS Auto Mode compute with `$.computeConfig.enabled` set to false.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to create or modify an Amazon EKS cluster
threats.threatAction: can encrypt the Kubernetes API data, such as Secrets and ConfigMaps, with key material outside the AWS account owner's control

threatContext.context: An IAM principal able to create your Amazon EKS cluster or associate an encryption configuration with it chooses the KMS key that encrypts the cluster's Kubernetes API data by setting `$.encryptionConfig[*].provider.keyArn`. If that key material sits outside your control, its holder can later revoke or delete it and leave that Kubernetes API data unreadable.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to create or modify an Amazon EKS cluster
threats.threatAction: can configure the cluster without required tagging information

threatContext.context: An IAM principal with permissions to create or modify an Amazon EKS cluster can omit the required tags, or later remove them through `UntagResource`. An Amazon EKS cluster left without those tags still serves the Kubernetes API and may fall outside ownership attribution, cost allocation, and compliance inventory.

threats.prerequisites: with knowledge of a flawed access entry or aws-auth ConfigMap mapping
threats.threatAction: can take advantage of the flawed access entry or aws-auth ConfigMap mapping to gain unauthorized access to the Amazon EKS cluster

threatContext.context: Your Amazon EKS cluster maps authenticated IAM principals to Kubernetes usernames and groups through access entries or the `aws-auth` ConfigMap. A defect in these mappings can let a threat actor gain unauthorized access to the Amazon EKS cluster.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to create or modify an Amazon EKS cluster's Kubernetes API data
threats.threatAction: can encrypt the Kubernetes API data with an AWS owned KMS key, limiting your ability to govern the key's policy and lifecycle and to audit key usage through CloudTrail

threatContext.context: An IAM principal able to create your Amazon EKS cluster's Kubernetes API data chooses whether the AWS owned key protects it at rest. You cannot govern that key's policy or lifecycle, and the service's use of it produces no CloudTrail events in your account.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to create or modify an Amazon EKS cluster that supports EKS Auto Mode compute and its EKS node monitoring agent
threats.threatAction: can create or configure the cluster without EKS Auto Mode compute and its EKS node monitoring agent enabled

threatContext.context: An IAM principal can create or modify your Amazon EKS cluster without ever enabling EKS Auto Mode compute and its EKS node monitoring agent. Without the agent's node-level health conditions and metrics, anomalous node activity, such as runaway process creation, an outbound traffic spike, or an unexpected iptables reject rule, blends into standard node readiness and pressure conditions.

threats.prerequisites: with unintended IAM permissions to read Kubernetes Secrets and other Kubernetes API data that an access entry or RBAC binding lets it read from an Amazon EKS cluster where the service uses grant-based KMS authorization
threats.threatAction: can read Kubernetes Secrets and other Kubernetes API data in the cluster because the KMS key policy cannot restrict which IAM principals can decrypt the data

threatContext.context: Amazon EKS decrypts your cluster's Kubernetes Secrets and other Kubernetes API data under a KMS grant it holds, so the key policy cannot restrict which principals read them. An IAM principal with unintended Kubernetes read permissions from an access entry's EKS access policies or an RBAC binding can read the plaintext data over HTTPS through the cluster's public or private Kubernetes API server endpoint.

threats.prerequisites: that has been granted access to an untrusted Amazon EKS cluster through an access entry created by that cluster's owner
threats.threatAction: can interact with the untrusted cluster over its Kubernetes API server endpoint, including sending workloads and data to it or receiving data from it

threatContext.context: The owner of an Amazon EKS cluster outside your organization can grant one of your IAM principals access through an access entry. That principal can then move data into or out of the cluster over its Kubernetes API server endpoint.

threats.prerequisites: who controls a VPC-connected resource in the same VPC as an Amazon EKS cluster
threats.threatAction: can interact with the cluster's private Kubernetes API server endpoint through overly permissive network rules and move laterally within the VPC

threatContext.context: When you enable private endpoint access, Amazon EKS serves the Kubernetes API server endpoint for your cluster through cross-account elastic network interfaces in your VPC. A threat actor controlling another resource in that VPC can reach that endpoint through overly permissive network rules and move laterally.

threats.prerequisites: with network access to an Amazon EKS cluster that permits traffic to services and administrative ports from unrestricted sources
threats.threatAction: can reach listening services and administrative ports on the cluster

threatContext.context: Amazon EKS attaches the cluster security group it creates, and any additional security groups you specify, to the network interfaces in your VPC that serve your cluster's private Kubernetes API server endpoint. An inbound rule permitting an unrestricted source range lets any host that can route to those interfaces reach their listening services.

threats.prerequisites: that has been granted access to my Amazon EKS cluster through its access entries
threats.threatAction: can use my Amazon EKS cluster

threatContext.context: Access entries on your Amazon EKS cluster can grant Kubernetes API access to principals outside your organization. Such a principal can authenticate to your cluster's Kubernetes API with its own IAM credentials. Depending on its entry's Kubernetes permissions, it can take actions such as reading Secrets or creating pods that run its code on your nodes.

threats.prerequisites: with Kubernetes access granted through an Amazon EKS access entry or the aws-auth ConfigMap that permits deleting Kubernetes objects, such as Secrets, ConfigMaps, workloads and PersistentVolumeClaims, from an Amazon EKS cluster
threats.threatAction: can delete Kubernetes objects, such as Secrets, ConfigMaps, workloads and PersistentVolumeClaims, or whole namespaces from the cluster

threatContext.context: Your Amazon EKS cluster's control plane stores Kubernetes objects, such as Secrets, ConfigMaps, workloads and PersistentVolumeClaims, each deletable through the Kubernetes API over HTTPS. An IAM principal with Kubernetes access granted through an Amazon EKS access entry or the `aws-auth` ConfigMap that permits deleting those objects can remove them individually or in whole namespaces while the cluster remains intact and stays active.

threats.prerequisites: with network access to an Amazon EKS cluster that has been placed in a public subnet
threats.threatAction: can access the cluster directly from an ungoverned network

threatContext.context: An Amazon EKS cluster receives network interfaces for its private Kubernetes API server endpoint in the subnets you choose for it, with globally unique IPv6 addresses by default in an IPv6 cluster. An Amazon EKS cluster placed in a subnet that routes to an internet gateway can be reached directly from an ungoverned network when those interfaces have a public IP address.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to create or update an Amazon EKS cluster's control plane instance and etcd instance
threats.threatAction: can configure the control plane instance and etcd instance to use an instance type that does not provide automatic encryption of instance-to-instance traffic

threatContext.context: An Amazon EKS cluster's AWS Outposts control plane and etcd instance type settings, `$.outpostConfig.controlPlaneInstanceType` and `$.outpostConfig.etcdInstanceType`, accept Amazon EC2 instance types that do not provide automatic encryption of instance-to-instance traffic. If such a type is selected, traffic between the cluster's instances themselves and other instances you operate can travel without that encryption.

threats.prerequisites: that has been granted access to my Amazon EKS cluster's service role, Auto Mode node IAM role, and connector agent IAM role through their trust policies
threats.threatAction: can assume my service role, Auto Mode node IAM role, and connector agent IAM role and act with their permissions

threatContext.context: Your Amazon EKS cluster designates its service role, Auto Mode node IAM role, and connector agent IAM role through `$.roleArn`, `$.computeConfig.nodeRoleArn`, `$.connectorConfig.roleArn`, and you author their trust policies. Those trust policies can allow identities outside your organization to assume the roles and act with their permissions.

threats.prerequisites: with possession of credentials for my Amazon EKS cluster's Auto Mode node IAM role or my registered external cluster's EKS Connector agent IAM role
threats.threatAction: can use my Auto Mode node IAM role or EKS Connector agent IAM role while on an unexpected network

threatContext.context: The instance metadata service on each EC2 managed instance serves credentials for your Auto Mode node IAM role, and AWS Systems Manager delivers credentials for your EKS Connector agent IAM role to the eks-connector agent. A threat actor who obtains those credentials can use either role while on an unexpected network.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to use an Amazon EKS cluster
threats.threatAction: can interact with the Kubernetes API without a record of their activities being persisted by control plane logging

threatContext.context: When control plane logging is not configured on your Amazon EKS cluster, no control plane logs are written by control plane logging to CloudWatch Logs. An IAM principal with permissions to use the cluster can make Kubernetes API requests that its Kubernetes permissions allow, leaving no record of those requests persisted by control plane logging.

threats.prerequisites: in possession of a long-lived, static Kubernetes service account token issued for an Amazon EKS cluster
threats.threatAction: can take advantage of the token to access the cluster

threatContext.context: Your Amazon EKS cluster's Kubernetes API server endpoint accepts Kubernetes service account tokens presented as bearer tokens in HTTPS requests. If you issue service account tokens to clients outside the cluster, such as CI/CD systems or external tools, anyone who obtains one of these tokens can authenticate as that service account and use its Kubernetes RBAC permissions from any network location that can reach the endpoint, including the internet if the public endpoint is enabled.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to modify an Amazon EKS cluster
threats.threatAction: can disable control plane logging, including the audit and authenticator log types, for the cluster

threatContext.context: An IAM principal with permissions to modify your Amazon EKS cluster can set `$.logging.clusterLogging[*].enabled` to `false` for selected log types by calling `UpdateClusterConfig`. That change stops the opt-in control plane logs of those types from reaching CloudWatch Logs while later Kubernetes API activity can continue unrecorded; limiting `$.logging.clusterLogging[*].types[*]` to `audit` and `authenticator` stops only those logs and leaves the other log types enabled.

threats.prerequisites: with control of an Amazon EKS cluster configured with overly permissive outbound security group rules
threats.threatAction: can use the cluster to interact with ungoverned network destinations

threatContext.context: Outbound rules on the security groups that Amazon EKS associates with the cluster's cross-account network interfaces in your subnets govern connections from those interfaces, which reach external endpoints only when the cluster's control plane egress mode is `CUSTOMER_ROUTED`. Where those rules permit an unrestricted destination range, a threat actor controlling the cluster can use it to interact with ungoverned network destinations.

threats.prerequisites: who can control the outbound connections of an Amazon EKS cluster using customer-routed control plane egress that is attached to a subnet with a route to an internet gateway
threats.threatAction: can send the cluster's outbound traffic directly to the public internet instead of through a governed network egress path

threatContext.context: With customer-routed control plane egress, your IPv6 cluster connects to external endpoints through network interfaces that Amazon EKS places in the cluster subnets you specify. Where those subnets route to an internet gateway, the control plane's connections can reach the public internet directly when those interfaces have a public IP address.

threats.prerequisites: with access to an Amazon EKS cluster
threats.threatAction: can submit a volume of requests that exceeds the capacity of the cluster or the network it is connected to

threatContext.context: With private endpoint access enabled, your Amazon EKS cluster receives Kubernetes API requests over HTTPS through its network interfaces in your subnets and has finite capacity. A threat actor who can reach it can send request volume that exhausts that capacity or the network it connects to.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to create or modify an Amazon EKS eks anywhere subscription
threats.threatAction: can configure the eks anywhere subscription without required tagging information

threatContext.context: An IAM principal with permissions to create or modify an Amazon EKS eks anywhere subscription can omit the required tags, or later remove them through `UntagResource`. An Amazon EKS eks anywhere subscription left without those tags still incurs charges for its term and may fall outside ownership attribution, cost allocation, and compliance inventory.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to create or modify an Amazon EKS cluster's fargate profile
threats.threatAction: can configure the fargate profile without required tagging information

threatContext.context: An IAM principal with permissions to create or modify an Amazon EKS cluster's fargate profile can omit the required tags, or remove them later through `UntagResource`. A fargate profile left without those tags still selects pods for AWS Fargate and may fall outside ownership attribution, cost allocation, and compliance inventory.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to create an Amazon EKS cluster's fargate profile
threats.threatAction: can create the fargate profile in a single Availability Zone

threatContext.context: An IAM principal with permissions to create an Amazon EKS cluster's fargate profile can set the subnet list in `$.subnets[*]` to place the profile's Pods in a single Availability Zone. An impairment of that zone can then leave those Pods without a healthy zone to run in and interrupt the services that depend on them.

threats.prerequisites: that has been granted access to my Amazon EKS cluster's Fargate profile's IAM Pod execution role through its trust policy
threats.threatAction: can assume my Pod execution role and act with its permissions

threatContext.context: Your Amazon EKS cluster's Fargate profile designates a Pod execution role through `$.podExecutionRoleArn`, and you author its trust policy. That trust policy can allow identities outside your organization to assume the role and act with its permissions.

threats.prerequisites: with possession of credentials for my Amazon EKS cluster's fargate profile's Pod execution role
threats.threatAction: can use my Pod execution role while on an unexpected network

threatContext.context: Amazon EKS provides temporary credentials for your fargate profile's Pod execution role to its own components that run your Pods on AWS Fargate. A threat actor who obtains those credentials can use that Pod execution role while on an unexpected network.
`CreateFargateProfile` allows you to specify a service role, referred to as the Pod execution role, for your Pod operations. The service uses the role to make AWS API calls from your code.

threats.prerequisites: who can execute code in Fargate Pods scheduled through an Amazon EKS cluster's fargate profile that is attached to a subnet with a route to an internet gateway
threats.threatAction: can send the Pods' outbound traffic directly to the public internet instead of through a governed network egress path

threatContext.context: After you call `CreateFargateProfile`, Amazon EKS launches the Pods your Fargate profile selects, with the network interfaces that carry their outbound traffic, in the subnets you specify. Where those subnets route to an internet gateway, code running in those Pods can reach the public internet directly when those interfaces have a public IP address.

threats.prerequisites: with network access to the Fargate Pods that an Amazon EKS cluster's fargate profile places in its subnets
threats.threatAction: can submit a volume of requests that exceeds the capacity of the Fargate Pods that the fargate profile places in its subnets or the network they are connected to

threatContext.context: Each Pod that your fargate profile schedules receives HTTP, HTTPS, TCP, UDP, or DNS requests on its own network interface in your subnets and has finite capacity. A threat actor who can reach it can send request volume that exhausts that capacity or the network it connects to.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to create or modify an Amazon EKS cluster's identity provider config
threats.threatAction: can configure the identity provider config without required tagging information

threatContext.context: An IAM principal with permissions to create or modify an Amazon EKS cluster's identity provider config can omit the required tags, or remove them later through `UntagResource`. An Amazon EKS cluster's identity provider config left without those tags still authenticates users to its cluster and may fall outside ownership attribution, cost allocation, and compliance inventory.

threats.prerequisites: with knowledge of a flawed OIDC identity provider configuration
threats.threatAction: can take advantage of the flawed OIDC identity provider configuration to gain unauthorized access to the Amazon EKS cluster

threatContext.context: Your Amazon EKS cluster's OIDC identity provider configuration maps the identities in ID tokens from the issuer you specify to Kubernetes users and groups. A defect in that configuration can let a threat actor gain unauthorized access to your cluster's Kubernetes API.

threats.prerequisites: with knowledge of a vulnerable Amazon EKS cluster's identity provider config
threats.threatAction: can gain federated access to the Kubernetes API server

threatContext.context: An Amazon EKS cluster's identity provider config delegates authentication for your cluster to the external OpenID Connect (OIDC) identity provider it names. If that identity provider is vulnerable, a threat actor presenting a signed ID token from that issuer can gain federated access to your Kubernetes API server.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to create or modify an Amazon EKS cluster's nodegroup
threats.threatAction: can configure the nodegroup without required tagging information

threatContext.context: An IAM principal with permissions to create or modify an Amazon EKS cluster's nodegroup can omit the required tags, or remove them through `UntagResource`. A nodegroup left without those tags still runs your cluster's workloads and may fall outside ownership attribution, cost allocation, and compliance inventory.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to create an Amazon EKS cluster's nodegroup
threats.threatAction: can create the nodegroup in a single Availability Zone

threatContext.context: An IAM principal with permissions to create an Amazon EKS cluster's nodegroup can use the subnets in `$.subnets[*]` to place every node and its network interfaces in a single Availability Zone. An impairment of that zone can then leave the nodegroup without a reachable node for the pods that can be scheduled only on it.

threats.prerequisites: who controls a VPC-connected resource in the same VPC as an Amazon EKS cluster's nodegroup
threats.threatAction: can interact with the nodegroup's worker node network interfaces through overly permissive network rules and move laterally within the VPC

threatContext.context: Your nodegroup's Amazon EC2 worker nodes have network interfaces in your VPC subnets that serve your workloads and any remote access you configure. A threat actor controlling another resource in that VPC can reach those interfaces through overly permissive network rules and move laterally.

threats.prerequisites: with network access to an Amazon EKS cluster's nodegroup that permits traffic to services and administrative ports from unrestricted sources
threats.threatAction: can reach listening services and administrative ports on the nodegroup

threatContext.context: The cluster security group or your launch template's security groups, plus any remote access security group, govern inbound traffic to your nodegroup's EC2 instances, which can have public IP addresses. An inbound rule permitting an unrestricted source range lets any host that can route to those instances reach their listening services and administrative ports.

threats.prerequisites: with network access to an Amazon EKS cluster's nodegroup that has been placed in a public subnet
threats.threatAction: can access the nodegroup directly from an ungoverned network

threatContext.context: An Amazon EKS cluster's nodegroup launches its Amazon EC2 worker nodes and their network interfaces into the subnets you specify when you create it. An Amazon EKS cluster's nodegroup placed in a subnet that routes to an internet gateway can be reached directly from an ungoverned network when those nodes have a public IP address.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to create or update an Amazon EKS cluster's nodegroup
threats.threatAction: can configure the nodegroup to use an instance type that does not provide automatic encryption of instance-to-instance traffic

threatContext.context: An Amazon EKS cluster's nodegroup's instance type settings, `$.instanceTypes[*]` and `$.LaunchTemplateData.InstanceType`, accept Amazon EC2 instance types that do not provide automatic encryption of instance-to-instance traffic. If such a type is selected, traffic between the nodegroup's instances themselves and other instances you operate can travel without that encryption.

threats.prerequisites: that has been granted access to my Amazon EKS cluster's nodegroup's node IAM role through its trust policy
threats.threatAction: can assume my node IAM role and act with its permissions

threatContext.context: Your Amazon EKS cluster's nodegroup designates a node IAM role through `$.nodeRole`, and you author its trust policy. That trust policy can allow identities outside your organization to assume the role and act with its permissions.

threats.prerequisites: with possession of credentials for my Amazon EKS cluster's nodegroup's node IAM role
threats.threatAction: can use my node IAM role while on an unexpected network

threatContext.context: The node IAM role that you specify on `CreateNodegroup` provides temporary credentials to every instance in your nodegroup through the instance metadata service. A threat actor who obtains those credentials can use that node IAM role while on an unexpected network.
`CreateNodegroup` allows you to specify a service role, referred to as the node IAM role, for your node operations. The service uses the role to make AWS API calls from your code.

threats.prerequisites: with control of an Amazon EKS cluster's nodegroup configured with overly permissive outbound security group rules
threats.threatAction: can use the nodegroup to interact with ungoverned network destinations

threatContext.context: Nodes in the nodegroup and their Pods connect through network interfaces associated with the cluster security group or security groups in the launch template, whose outbound rules govern those connections. Where those rules permit an unrestricted destination range, a threat actor controlling the nodegroup can use it to interact with ungoverned network destinations.

threats.prerequisites: who can execute code in an Amazon EKS cluster's nodegroup that is attached to a subnet with a route to an internet gateway
threats.threatAction: can send the nodegroup's outbound traffic directly to the public internet instead of through a governed network egress path

threatContext.context: When you call `CreateNodegroup`, Amazon EKS launches your nodegroup's worker nodes, with the network interfaces that carry their outbound traffic, in the subnets you specify. Where those subnets route to an internet gateway, code running on those nodes or in their Pods can reach the public internet directly when those interfaces have a public IP address.

threats.prerequisites: with access to an Amazon EKS cluster's nodegroup
threats.threatAction: can submit a volume of requests that exceeds the capacity of the nodegroup or the network it is connected to

threatContext.context: Each node that your nodegroup launches into your subnets receives HTTP, HTTPS, DNS, TCP, and UDP traffic on its network interfaces and has finite capacity. A threat actor who can reach it can send request volume that exhausts that capacity or the network it connects to.

threats.prerequisites: with IAM permissions to create or modify an Amazon EKS cluster's pod identity association
threats.threatAction: can configure the pod identity association without required tagging information

threatContext.context: An IAM principal with permissions to create or modify an Amazon EKS cluster's pod identity association can omit the required tags, or remove them later through `UntagResource`. A pod identity association left without those tags still provides IAM role credentials and may fall outside ownership attribution, cost allocation, and compliance inventory.

threats.prerequisites: that has been granted access to my Amazon EKS cluster's pod identity association's IAM EKS Pod Identity role through its trust policy
threats.threatAction: can assume my EKS Pod Identity role and act with its permissions

threatContext.context: Your Amazon EKS cluster's pod identity association designates an EKS Pod Identity role through `$.roleArn`, and you author its trust policy. That trust policy can allow identities outside your organization to assume the role and act with its permissions, accessing the AWS resources your workloads use.
